target: AG1’s claim that AI is broadly good because it makes daily life easier, improves health and education, helps marginalized users, and increases workplace safety
objection: AG2 argues that this convenience-focused case ignores major harms from AI at scale: job displacement and wage pressure, medical errors and opaque decision-making, weakened student critical thinking, biased or exclusionary accessibility tools, and expanded workplace surveillance and privacy loss.

target: AG2’s claim that AI’s harms are inevitable consequences of deployment
objection: AG1 objects that AG2 treats harms as unavoidable when they are actually manageable through responsible design and governance, such as retraining workers, human oversight in healthcare, learning-focused tutoring, bias monitoring, privacy-preserving workplace safety tools, and inclusive evaluation.

target: AG1’s argument that governance and better design can fix AI’s harms
objection: AG2 counters that mitigation is not reliably achievable in practice because incentives and system design push toward broader data extraction, accountability is diffused across vendors and users, critical-thinking damage is cultural as well as instructional, and bias in high-stakes systems is not solved by training tweaks alone.

target: AG2’s claim that incentives and institutional messiness make mitigation ineffective
objection: AG1 replies that this assumes harms are inevitable rather than manageable and underestimates how policy can redirect incentives, impose privacy limits, assign legal responsibility, structure AI use so it reinforces learning, and improve fairness through ongoing evaluation.

target: AG1’s claim that governance can keep pace with AI deployment
objection: AG2 argues that responsible deployment is not a stable equilibrium because adoption outpaces enforcement, privacy-friendly design conflicts with data-hungry model training and business value, accountability mechanisms become superficial paperwork, and educational use still shifts people toward outsourcing reasoning.

target: AG2’s claim that enforcement lags, privacy conflicts with performance, accountability gets gamed, and educational reliance will still erode skills
objection: AG1 objects that these are not reasons AI is inherently bad; they are reasons to use phase-gated deployment, privacy-by-design, meaningful audits and liability, and assessment designs that require students to show their reasoning.

target: AG1’s proposed fixes of certification, continuous monitoring, and privacy-friendly architectures
objection: AG2 responds that these fixes fail in the market: certification and audits favor large firms and increase concentration, model updates make audits go stale, and privacy-by-design conflicts with prevailing business models that reward behavioral tracking and personalization.

target: AG2’s claim that market and lifecycle realities defeat governance
objection: AG1 argues that governance and product architecture can be redesigned to match incentives, including shared certification resources, continuous monitoring and rollback, and privacy-preserving personalization so companies need not rely on open-ended data hoarding.

target: AG1’s proposal that governance can be redesigned to solve market and lifecycle problems
objection: AG2 says the proposed fixes still fail in practice because shared certification can become industry capture, continuous monitoring often requires more data and thus more surveillance, on-device/privacy-friendly approaches are not universal, and competitive pressure still pushes scope creep.

target: AG2’s claim that certification, monitoring, and privacy-friendly design cannot work reliably
objection: AG1 objects that monitoring can be done with minimized or anonymized telemetry, independent regulators and third-party labs can prevent capture, hybrid on-device/cloud architectures can preserve privacy, and not using AI also imposes harms on people who benefit from accessibility, health, and safety tools.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy-preserving monitoring and independent oversight can reliably reduce harms
objection: AG2 argues that even minimized telemetry can enable re-identification, representative audits miss rare or contextual harms, and independent regulators or labs are still subject to institutional incentives and resource limits, so the privacy and bias failure modes remain.

target: AG2’s conclusion that imperfect controls mean AI is not good for society
objection: AG1 objects that society should judge AI by expected net benefit under risk controls rather than by impossible zero-harm standards, and that stronger privacy, better testing, and diversified oversight can make AI net-positive.

target: AG1’s claim that risk-tiering, human accountability, and better oversight make AI socially beneficial
objection: AG2 argues that risk-tiering breaks down when AI components are recombined into other products and workflows, harms are externalized onto non-users who did not consent, and even reduced privacy still leaves a pervasive tracking ecosystem.

target: AG2’s claim that recombination, externalities, and residual tracking make AI bad overall
objection: AG1 says those are reasons for ecosystem-level safeguards, not for rejecting AI: downstream governance can constrain recombination through licensing and technical controls, existing law can address externalities like discrimination and labor disruption, and many AI benefits do not require pervasive surveillance.

target: AG1’s claim that downstream governance and existing law can manage recombination and externalities
objection: AG2 replies that licensing and access controls cannot stop repackaging or repurposing when incentives are strong, legal remedies are too slow and hard to enforce for many harms, and the benefits are unevenly distributed while burdens fall disproportionately on workers, minorities, and the public.

target: AG2’s claim that governance and law cannot reliably constrain recombination and unequal harms
objection: AG1 counters that recombination can be constrained with technical and procedural measures such as restricted APIs, provenance/version tracking, and procurement rules; that law can reduce baseline harm rates even if it is imperfect; and that uneven harms call for targeted mitigation rather than abandoning AI.

target: AG1’s claim that lifecycle-aware governance and mitigation can make AI net-good
objection: AG2 argues that some of the biggest harms are hard-to-measure tail risks like misinformation and manipulation, provenance does not stop power-driven misuse, and AI concentrates power and dependency in the hands of model owners and distributors.

target: AG2’s claim that tail risks and power concentration make AI net-bad
objection: AG1 objects that tail risks can be directly mitigated with provenance, source labeling, retrieval/citation requirements, and human review; that prevention controls like rate limits and output filtering can reduce misuse before it scales; and that policy and public-sector adoption can counter concentration while preserving benefits.

target: AG1’s claim that provenance, filtering, human approval, and policy can sufficiently reduce AI harms
objection: AG2 responds that watermarks and source labels can be removed or degraded, filtering and human review miss novel failure modes and suffer from automation bias, anti-monopoly and public-interest measures are too slow to offset rapid deployment, and routine AI use erodes critical agency and trust over time.
